title: What is a "distributed monolith" (services that deploy/fail/scale together via shared libraries, shared DBs, synchronous chains), and how do you avoid it?
shortTitle: What is a "distributed monolith," and how do you avoid it?
keyPoints: A distributed monolith has the complexity of distribution with none of the independence of microservices.
Symptom 1: shared database -- schema changes force coordinated simultaneous redeploys.
Symptom 2: shared libraries with business logic -- changing the library forces rebuilding every consumer.
Symptom 3: long synchronous call chains -- latency is the sum and availability is the product of all hops.
Fix: database-per-service, share contracts not code, prefer async events, add resilience to sync calls.
If you cannot cleanly separate data and deployment, the services were probably split along wrong boundaries.
Starting as a modular monolith and extracting only when needed is the safer path.

s1_definition.oneliner: A distributed monolith is microservices that still deploy, fail, and scale together through shared databases, shared code, and synchronous call chains, giving you all the complexity of distribution with none of the independence.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Shared database** -- several services read/write the same tables, so a schema change forces coordinated simultaneous redeploys.
- **Shared business-logic library** -- changing the library forces rebuilding and redeploying every consumer, destroying independent deployment.
- **Synchronous call chains** -- A calls B calls C calls D; latency is the sum, availability is the product, and one slow service cascades failure backward.
- **Temporal coupling** -- services must deploy in a specific order or all at once; they are not independently deployable.
- **Fix** -- database-per-service, share contracts not code, prefer async events, add resilience to remaining sync calls, evolve APIs backward-compatibly.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India split one giant department into several to be modern, but chained them so tightly that nothing improved. They share one filing cabinet (shared DB), all use the same rulebook binder (shared library), and to approve one loan the loan clerk must phone the account clerk who must phone the fraud clerk (sync chain). If any clerk is on break the whole approval freezes. The bank now has many departments with all the coordination headaches and still fails as one.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Distributed Monolith (the problem)
  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
  │ Service A│  │ Service B│  │ Service C│
  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘
       │             │             │
       └──────┬──────┘──────┬──────┘
              ▼             ▼
        ┌──────────┐  ┌────────────┐
        │Shared DB │  │Shared Lib  │
        └──────────┘  └────────────┘
  Schema change breaks all three
  Library change forces all to rebuild

  Fixed Architecture
  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
  │ Service A│  │ Service B│  │ Service C│
  │ own DB-A │  │ own DB-B │  │ own DB-C │
  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘  └────┬─────┘
       │    events    │    API     │
       └──────────────┘────────────┘
  Each deploys independently
  Schema changes are local
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A distributed monolith has been split across the network but still cannot deploy, fail, or scale independently, giving you all the operational complexity of microservices with none of their benefits. The symptoms are a shared database where schema changes force coordinated redeploys, shared libraries with business logic that force lockstep rebuilds, and long synchronous call chains where one slow service cascades failure backward.

The fixes are concrete: database-per-service so each service owns its data exclusively, share contracts (API and event schemas) not code, prefer async events over sync chains, and add resilience patterns to any remaining sync calls. Evolve APIs backward-compatibly so services can deploy in any order.

At National Bank of India, the distributed monolith showed up clearly: four services shared one database, and loan approval was a sync chain through account, fraud, and credit. Pankaj fixed it by giving each service its own database, moving fraud and account checks onto Kafka, and wrapping the remaining credit check in a circuit breaker. If you genuinely cannot separate the data, the services were split along the wrong boundaries and the right move is to merge them back.

Remember one sentence: a distributed monolith is microservices that deploy, fail, and scale together through shared databases, shared code, and sync chains, and you fix it by isolating each service's data, sharing contracts not code, and decoupling with async events.
